statement: Data flow diagrams exist for key systems and show how data moves between systems and across internal and external boundaries, including third parties. The diagrams are updated when a significant system or network change occurs and reviewed on a defined cycle. Proof is the dated diagrams and the network diagram of authorized communication paths.
why_asked: If nobody knows where data travels, unprotected flows, shadow connections and third-party exposure stay invisible.
how_to_ask: Ask for the diagram of a key system and trace one flow out of the organization. Check the date. Example probe: "Where does customer data leave this system, to whom, and when was this diagram last updated?"
question: Does your organization keep current maps of how data moves between key systems and across its boundaries?
expected_evidence: Data flow diagrams for key systems; network diagram showing authorized communication paths and external connections; documentation of expected ports, protocols and services; version history; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: Diagrams cover each key system and show internal and external flows, including third parties. Authorized paths, ports, protocols and services are documented. Diagrams are dated after the latest significant change.
test: Obtain the diagrams and the change log. Sample three key systems and check each has a diagram showing internal and external flows. Check each diagram is dated after the latest significant change. Pass if all sampled diagrams are present and current.
baseline_risk: Unknown data paths bypass controls, and a breach cannot be scoped quickly because nobody knows where the data went.

statement: Every asset in the inventory is ranked by its criticality, the resources it needs and its impact on the mission, in addition to its classification. Written criteria set the ranking, the resulting priority is recorded on each asset, and priorities are reviewed on a defined cycle and after significant organizational change. This does not repeat the classification scheme. Proof is the criteria and the inventory with priorities.
why_asked: Without a priority on each asset, protection and recovery effort is spread evenly instead of going first to what the business cannot lose.
how_to_ask: Ask for the priority criteria, then open the inventory and look for the rating on a sample of assets. Example probe: "Pick a server. Where does the inventory show how important it is, and who decided that?"
question: Does your organization give each asset a reviewed priority based on its criticality and mission impact?
expected_evidence: Asset prioritization criteria; asset inventory showing a priority or criticality rating on each asset; version history showing the latest review; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: Written criteria weigh classification, criticality, resources and mission impact. Every asset has a priority. Priorities were reviewed within the cycle or after a significant change.
test: Obtain the criteria and the inventory. Check the criteria cover the four factors. Sample ten assets and check each carries a priority. Check the version history shows a review in the period. Pass if all sampled assets are rated and a review is dated in the period.
baseline_risk: Recovery and protection effort goes to the wrong assets, so the most critical systems suffer the longest outages.

statement: Security procedures are documented for each stage of an asset life cycle: acquisition or deployment, change, and retirement. The procedures require assets to be built to a secure baseline before going live and require data destruction when hardware is retired, reassigned or sent for repair. Records show the procedures were followed. Proof is the procedures, build records and the disposal log.
why_asked: Security steps skipped at deployment or disposal leave assets misconfigured when they go live and leak data when they leave.
how_to_ask: Ask for the procedure for each stage, then ask for one recent deployment and one disposal. Example probe: "Show me the build record for a system deployed last quarter and the disposal record for one retired."
question: Does your organization set security steps for each stage of an asset life cycle, from deployment through change to retirement?
expected_evidence: Asset life cycle procedures for acquisition, change and retirement; secure configuration baselines; build or change records for deployed systems; disposal and sanitization log; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: Procedures cover acquisition or deployment, change and retirement. Data destruction is required when hardware is retired, reassigned or repaired. Build records show systems met the baseline before go-live. Disposal records exist for retired assets.
test: Obtain the procedures, build records and disposal log. Sample three systems deployed in the period and check each shows baseline configuration before go-live. Sample three retired assets and check each has a disposal or sanitization record. Pass if all sampled records exist.
baseline_risk: Assets enter service insecure or leave with data still on them.

statement: Unsupported software is avoided in production, or an exception with a replacement plan is recorded. Software that is unauthorized or not needed is removed. Proof is the inventory with support status, exception records and removal records.
why_asked: Software the vendor no longer supports gets no security fixes, and unneeded software widens the attack surface.
how_to_ask: Ask for a report of unsupported software and what is done about each item. Example probe: "Which software in production is past vendor support, and where is the replacement plan or exception for each?"
question: Does your organization avoid unsupported software in production and remove software it does not need?
expected_evidence: Software inventory showing support status; end-of-life exceptions and replacement plans for software; software inventory review with removal records. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: No unsupported software runs in production without a recorded exception and replacement plan. Unauthorized or unneeded software found in reviews was removed, with a record.
test: Obtain the software inventory with support status and the exception records. Sample software past vendor support and software removals from the review period. Pass if each sampled unsupported item has a replacement plan or recorded exception, and each sampled removal is recorded.
baseline_risk: Unsupported software runs with unpatched flaws that attackers exploit, and unneeded software widens the attack surface.

statement: A documented procedure covers hardware replacement at end of life and secure disposal. Hardware past vendor support has a replacement plan or a recorded exception. Retired hardware is disposed of securely, with data sanitization recorded in a disposal log.
why_asked: Hardware past vendor support gets no fixes, and retired devices that are not wiped leak the data they held.
how_to_ask: Ask for hardware past vendor support and the disposal log for the period. Example probe: "Which hardware is past vendor support, and for the last device retired, where is the wipe record?"
question: Does your organization plan replacement of hardware before vendor support ends and dispose of retired hardware securely?
expected_evidence: Hardware replacement and disposal procedure; asset inventory showing hardware support status; replacement plans or exceptions for hardware; disposal log with data sanitization evidence. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: A procedure covers replacement and disposal. Hardware past support has a replacement plan or recorded exception. Every retired device has a disposal record with sanitization evidence.
test: Obtain the procedure, the inventory with support status and the disposal log. Sample hardware past vendor support and hardware retired in the review period. Pass if the procedure exists, each sampled aging item has a replacement plan or recorded exception, and each retired item has disposal and sanitization evidence.
baseline_risk: Unsupported hardware stays in service with unfixable flaws, and retired devices leak the data they held.
